## Bad Faith Bankruptcy Filing - What It Means
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/bad-faith-filing.html

bankruptcydenied.com

Bad Faith Bankruptcy Filing

Filing bankruptcy for improper purposes - to delay creditors, abuse the system, or gain unfair advantage - can result in dismissal and refiling restrictions.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Bad Faith Bankruptcy Filing - What It Means

What is bad faith?

Under 11 U.S.C. § 707(b)(3) (Chapter 7) and § 1325(a)(3) (Chapter 13), the court evaluates whether the filing was made in good faith. There is no single definition of bad faith - courts look at the totality of the circumstances.

Common indicators of bad faith include:

Serial filings. Filing repeatedly to abuse the automatic stay and delay creditors without genuine intent to reorganize or obtain a discharge. See serialfiler.org.

Filing on the eve of foreclosure. Filing solely to delay a scheduled foreclosure sale, with no ability to propose a viable plan.

Concealing assets or income. Filing while hiding property or understating income.

Timing manipulation. Strategically filing to exploit lookback periods or to defeat a specific creditor action.

No genuine financial distress. Filing when you can actually pay your debts but prefer not to.

Consequences of bad faith finding

Case dismissal under § 707(b) or § 1307(c)

180-day refiling bar under § 109(g)

In extreme cases, a permanent injunction against refiling without court permission

Sanctions or attorney fee awards to affected creditors

How courts evaluate good faith

Courts typically consider factors including: accuracy and completeness of the petition, whether the debtor has a genuine need for relief, the debtor's payment history, whether the filing was timed to abuse the process, and the debtor's overall conduct. Good faith is evaluated case by case.

Serial filings trigger special rules. Under 11 U.S.C. § 362(c)(3), if you had a case dismissed within the past year, the automatic stay in your new case lasts only 30 days (instead of for the duration of the case). If you had two or more cases dismissed within the past year, § 362(c)(4) provides no automatic stay at all - you must file a motion and prove good faith to get stay protection.

Related Guides

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Bankruptcy Dismissed - What Now?

File Bankruptcy Again Guide

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

Most unsecured debts are discharged, including credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, and utility arrears. Debts that typically cannot be discharged include student loans (except in hardship cases), most taxes, child support, alimony, and debts from fraud or willful injury.

## Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Denial - Why Cases Get Dismissed
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/chapter-7-denial.html

bankruptcydenied.com

Ch. 7 Denial

Prior Dismissal

Chapter 7 Denial - Why Cases Get Dismissed

Chapter 7 cases can be dismissed for abuse, means test failure, bad faith, or procedural failures. Here is what triggers dismissal.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Chapter 7 Bankruptcy Denial - Why Cases Get Dismi

Grounds for Chapter 7 dismissal

Under 11 U.S.C. § 707, the court can dismiss a Chapter 7 case for several reasons:

1. Means test failure (§ 707(b)(2))

The means test compares your income to your state's median income. If your income exceeds the median and the means test formula shows you can repay a significant portion of your debts, the case is presumed to be an abuse. See our means test failure guide.

2. Totality of circumstances abuse (§ 707(b)(3))

Even if you pass the means test, the court can dismiss for abuse based on the totality of your circumstances. Indicators include: ability to pay debts from future income, recent lavish spending, or strategically timing income to manipulate the means test.

3. Bad faith (§ 707(b)(3)(A))

Filing in bad faith - to delay creditors, to abuse the process, or for improper purposes - is grounds for dismissal. See our bad faith guide.

4. Failure to comply with filing requirements

Under § 521, you must file all required documents within specified deadlines. Failure to provide tax returns, pay stubs, credit counseling certificates, or complete schedules can result in automatic dismissal.

5. Prior discharge time bar

Under 11 U.S.C. § 727(a)(8), you cannot receive a Chapter 7 discharge if you received one in a prior Chapter 7 case filed within 8 years. Under § 1328(f), a prior Chapter 13 discharge within 6 years bars a Chapter 7 discharge (with exceptions).

What happens after dismissal?

When a Chapter 7 case is dismissed, the automatic stay lifts and creditors can resume collection. You can typically refile unless the court orders otherwise under § 109(g). If the dismissal is for abuse, the court may impose a 180-day bar on refiling or conditions on any future filing.

Conversion is often an option. If your Chapter 7 case is at risk of dismissal for means test failure, you may be able to convert to Chapter 13 under 11 U.S.C. § 706(a). Chapter 13 does not have a means test - instead, your income determines your plan payment amount.

Related Guides

Bankruptcy Dismissed - What Now?

File Bankruptcy Again Guide

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

While bankruptcy is federal law, each state sets its own exemptions that determine what property you can keep. Some states also allow you to choose between state and federal exemptions. Your state's median income determines Chapter 7 eligibility through the means test.

## Bankruptcy Denial FAQ
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/faq.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial

FAQ

Bankruptcy Denial FAQ

Common questions about what happens when bankruptcy does not go as planned.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Bankruptcy Denial FAQ

Frequently asked questions

How many times can you file bankruptcy?

There is no statutory limit on filings. You can file as many times as you want. But you can only receive a discharge within certain time limits: 8 years between Chapter 7 discharges, 6 years between Chapter 13 and Chapter 7 (with exceptions), 4 years between Chapter 7 and Chapter 13, and 2 years between Chapter 13 discharges. Check 1328f.com for the specific time bars under 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f).

Can a creditor object to my discharge?

Yes. Under 11 U.S.C. § 727(c), the trustee, a creditor, or the U.S. Trustee can object to your discharge. The complaint must be filed within 60 days after the first date set for the 341 meeting under Bankruptcy Rule 4004(a).

What is the difference between discharge denial and nondischargeability?

Discharge denial under § 727 means none of your debts are discharged - you get no fresh start at all. Nondischargeability under § 523 means specific debts survive while the rest are discharged. You can lose the battle on one debt but still win the war on everything else.

Does a dismissed bankruptcy hurt my credit?

Yes. The filing itself appears on your credit report for 7 to 10 years, regardless of whether it results in a discharge or dismissal. However, a dismissed case may actually look worse than a completed case to some lenders, because it suggests the filing failed.

Can I refile immediately after dismissal?

Usually, unless the court imposed a 180-day bar under § 109(g). But be aware that repeat filings within a year trigger reduced automatic stay under § 362(c)(3)-(4). You may need to file a motion for stay protection in the new case.

What if my Chapter 13 plan is denied confirmation?

You can amend the plan and resubmit it. Most courts allow multiple amendments. If the plan cannot be made to work, you can convert to Chapter 7 (if you qualify) or the case will be dismissed under § 1307(c).

Can I get my filing fee back if the case is denied?

No. Filing fees are not refundable. The Chapter 7 filing fee is $338 and the Chapter 13 filing fee is $313. If you qualify as low-income, you may be able to file a fee waiver application under 28 U.S.C. § 1930(f).

Related Guides

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Bankruptcy Dismissed - What Now?

File Bankruptcy Again Guide

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

There is no limit on the number of times you can file. However, time bars under 11 U.S.C. Section 727(a)(8)-(9) and Section 1328(f) restrict how often you can receive a discharge. Serial filings also trigger reduced automatic stay protection.

## Fraud and Concealment in Bankruptcy - Discharge Denial
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/fraud-concealment.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing
Fraud
What to Do
FAQ

Fraud and Concealment - Discharge Denial

Hiding assets, lying under oath, or destroying financial records can permanently cost you your bankruptcy discharge.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Fraud and Concealment in Bankruptcy - Discharge D

Grounds for discharge denial

11 U.S.C. § 727(a) lists specific grounds for denying a debtor's discharge entirely. Unlike case dismissal (which lets you refile), discharge denial means all your debts survive the bankruptcy permanently for that case.

The statutory grounds

§ 727(a)(2): Transferring, destroying, or concealing property with intent to defraud, within 1 year before filing or during the case

§ 727(a)(3): Concealing, destroying, mutilating, or failing to keep adequate financial records

§ 727(a)(4): Making a false oath or account - this includes any false statement on your petition, schedules, or at the 341 meeting

§ 727(a)(5): Failing to satisfactorily explain any loss of assets or deficiency of assets to meet liabilities

§ 727(a)(6): Refusing to obey a lawful court order or refusing to testify (invoking Fifth Amendment after being granted immunity)

Criminal penalties

Beyond losing your discharge, bankruptcy fraud is a federal crime:

18 U.S.C. § 152: Concealment of assets, false oaths, false claims, and other fraudulent acts in bankruptcy cases are punishable by up to 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

The U.S. Trustee's office actively monitors for fraud and refers cases to the U.S. Attorney for prosecution. The Department of Justice Bankruptcy Fraud Initiative processes hundreds of referrals per year.

How fraud is discovered

Bank statement analysis. Trustees compare deposits against reported income and look for hidden accounts.

Public records searches. Property records, vehicle registrations, business filings, and court records reveal undisclosed assets.

Creditor tips. Creditors who know about hidden assets can inform the trustee.

Social media. Posts showing expensive purchases, travel, or lifestyle inconsistent with the petition.

Cross-referencing tax returns. Comparing IRS records against the petition reveals omitted income, assets, and transfers.

Discharge denial is permanent for the case. Once denied, there is no appeal or do-over within the same case. You may be able to file a new case in the future (subject to time bars and any refiling restrictions), but you will carry the stigma of a prior denial - and the court in the new case will scrutinize everything closely.

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

A bankruptcy mill is a high-volume law firm that processes large numbers of bankruptcy cases with minimal attorney involvement. Cases are often handled by paralegals or software, leading to errors, missed deadlines, and poor outcomes for clients.

## Incomplete Paperwork - When Bankruptcy Is Dismissed for Missing Documents
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/incomplete-paperwork.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing

FAQ

Incomplete Paperwork - Procedural Dismissal

Filing bankruptcy requires extensive documentation. Missing deadlines or omitting required documents leads to automatic dismissal.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Incomplete Paperwork - When Bankruptcy Is Dismiss

Required documents and deadlines

Under 11 U.S.C. § 521, the debtor must file a substantial set of documents:

Schedules A/B through J - assets, liabilities, income, expenses, executory contracts

Statement of Financial Affairs (SOFA) - comprehensive financial history

Means test form (Chapter 7) or Chapter 13 plan

Credit counseling certificate - must be completed within 180 days before filing

Tax returns - most recent year filed, provided to the trustee at least 7 days before the 341 meeting

Pay stubs - 60 days of pay advices, provided to the trustee before the 341 meeting

Photo ID and SSN verification - presented at the 341 meeting

If schedules are not filed within 14 days of the petition (or an extended deadline), the case is automatically dismissed under § 521(i).

Common procedural failures

Missing the credit counseling requirement. Under § 109(h), you must complete a course from an approved provider before filing. Filing without it renders the petition deficient.

Failing to provide tax returns. Under § 521(e)(2), failure to provide tax returns to the trustee can result in dismissal.

Incomplete schedules. Leaving assets off Schedule A/B, omitting creditors from Schedules D/E/F, or failing to list income sources will draw trustee scrutiny and potential dismissal.

Missing the 341 meeting. Failure to attend is grounds for dismissal. See what happens if you miss it.

How to avoid procedural dismissal

Gather all required documents before filing - do not file first and gather later

Complete credit counseling before your attorney files the petition

Provide tax returns and pay stubs to the trustee promptly

Respond to all trustee requests within the stated deadline

If you need more time, file a motion for extension before the deadline passes

Procedural dismissals are usually fixable. If your case is dismissed for incomplete paperwork, you can typically refile after gathering the missing documents. There is generally no bar on refiling for procedural dismissals (unlike bad-faith dismissals).

## Bankruptcy Denied? - What to Do Next [2026]
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/

Skip to main content

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing
Fraud
What to Do
FAQ

Bankruptcy Denied?

Yes. Your case can be dismissed, your plan can be denied confirmation, and your discharge can be refused. Here is why it happens and what you can do about it.

~33%
Ch. 13 cases dismissed (national avg)

180 days
Potential refiling bar after dismissal

8 years
Ch. 7 to Ch. 7 discharge bar

Yes. Your Chapter 7 case can be dismissed for means test failure, abuse, or bad faith. Your discharge can be denied for fraud, concealment, or false statements. Chapter 13 cases can be denied confirmation if the plan does not meet legal requirements.

Three ways bankruptcy can fail

When people ask "can bankruptcy be denied?" they usually mean one of three different things:

Case dismissal. The court throws out your case before you get a discharge. Common reasons: failing the means test, incomplete paperwork, bad faith filing, or violating court orders. National bankruptcy dismissal statistics show significant variation across districts and attorneys.

Discharge denial. Your case proceeds, but the court refuses to grant you a discharge. This means all your debts survive. Grounds include fraud, concealment, and false statements under 11 U.S.C. § 727(a).

Plan denial (Chapter 13). The court refuses to confirm your Chapter 13 plan because it does not meet the legal requirements of 11 U.S.C. § 1325. You can amend and resubmit, but repeated failures lead to dismissal.

Common reasons for denial

Chapter 7 Denial

Means test failure, totality of circumstances abuse, and other reasons your Chapter 7 case can be dismissed.

Means Test Failure

How the means test works, what happens if you fail it, and your options if your income is too high for Chapter 7.

Bad Faith Filing

What constitutes bad faith in bankruptcy. Serial filings, timing abuse, and filing to delay creditors.

Prior Dismissal

How a prior dismissal affects your new case. Reduced automatic stay, refiling bars, and repeat filer rules.

Incomplete Paperwork

Missing documents, unfiled schedules, and procedural failures that lead to case dismissal.

Fraud and Concealment

How hiding assets, lying under oath, and destroying records can result in permanent denial of discharge.

What to Do If Denied

Your options after denial - refiling, converting to another chapter, appealing, or negotiating with creditors.

FAQ

Common questions about bankruptcy denial, dismissal, and what happens next.

Discharge denial is permanent for that case. If the court denies your discharge under § 727(a), there is no second chance in that case. All debts survive. You may be able to refile a new case in the future (subject to time bars), but the denial stands for the current case.

Dismissal is usually not the end. Most dismissals are for procedural reasons (incomplete paperwork, missed deadlines) that can be corrected. You can typically refile after fixing the problems, unless the court imposes a bar on refiling.

## Means Test Failure - What Happens If You Fail
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/means-test-failure.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing
Fraud
What to Do
FAQ

Means Test Failure - Now What?

Failing the means test does not mean you cannot file bankruptcy. It means Chapter 7 may not be available - but you have options.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Means Test Failure - What Happens If You Fail

How the means test works

The means test under 11 U.S.C. § 707(b)(2) is a two-step income analysis:

Step 1: Compare your income to the state median. If your current monthly income (averaged over the 6 months before filing) is below your state's median income for your household size, you pass. No further analysis needed.

Step 2: Calculate disposable income. If your income exceeds the median, subtract allowed expenses (IRS standards, actual secured debt payments, and other deductions). If the result shows you could pay at least $8,175 over 60 months (or 25% of your unsecured debt), a presumption of abuse arises.

What the presumption of abuse means

If the means test creates a presumption of abuse, it does not automatically dismiss your case. The U.S. Trustee reviews the results and may file a motion to dismiss under § 707(b). You then have the opportunity to rebut the presumption by showing "special circumstances" that justify additional expenses or income adjustments.

Special circumstances can include: serious medical conditions, call to active military duty, or other documented, unusual expenses that the standard means test does not capture.

Your options if you fail

Rebut the presumption. Show special circumstances that reduce your disposable income below the threshold.

Convert to Chapter 13. Chapter 13 has no means test. Your income determines your plan payment, not your eligibility. Under 11 U.S.C. § 706(a), you have the right to convert.

Wait and refile. If your income is temporarily high (overtime, bonus, seasonal work), waiting until it normalizes may change the means test result. The test uses a 6-month lookback.

Adjust deductions. Legitimate increases in expenses - higher mortgage payments, medical costs, childcare - can change the calculation.

Failing the means test is not the end. Chapter 13 is available regardless of income, and many people who fail the means test successfully complete Chapter 13 plans. The means test only gates access to Chapter 7 - it does not prevent bankruptcy relief entirely.

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

While bankruptcy is federal law, each state sets its own exemptions that determine what property you can keep. Some states also allow you to choose between state and federal exemptions. Your state's median income determines Chapter 7 eligibility through the means test.

## Prior Bankruptcy Dismissal - How It Affects Your New Case
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/prior-dismissal.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing
Fraud
What to Do
FAQ

Prior Dismissal and Refiling

If your previous bankruptcy was dismissed, your new case faces special rules. Reduced stay protection, refiling bars, and heightened scrutiny.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›Prior Bankruptcy Dismissal - How It Affects Your

The 180-day refiling bar

Under 11 U.S.C. § 109(g), a debtor may not file a new bankruptcy case within 180 days of a dismissal if the prior case was dismissed for:

Willful failure to abide by court orders

Willful failure to appear before the court

Voluntary dismissal after a creditor filed a motion for relief from the automatic stay

If none of these apply, there is generally no automatic waiting period before refiling. But the court in the new case will closely examine the circumstances of the prior dismissal.

Reduced automatic stay

The most significant consequence of a prior dismissal is reduced automatic stay protection in your new case:

SituationAutomatic Stay DurationSection

No prior dismissalFull stay (duration of case)§ 362(a)

1 dismissal in past year30 days only (unless extended by court)§ 362(c)(3)

2+ dismissals in past yearNo stay at all (must petition court)§ 362(c)(4)

To extend the stay beyond 30 days (or to obtain one at all with 2+ dismissals), you must file a motion within the first 30 days and demonstrate that the new case was filed in good faith.

Proving good faith after a dismissal

Courts look at whether your circumstances have changed since the dismissed case. Factors include:

Did your financial situation change (job loss, medical emergency)?

Did you address the problems that caused the prior dismissal?

Are you filing to reorganize genuinely, or just to delay?

How many prior filings have you had?

Time bars from prior discharges are separate from dismissal rules. If your prior case resulted in a discharge (not just a dismissal), you must also satisfy the time bars under 11 U.S.C. § 727(a)(8)-(9) and § 1328(f). A dismissal without discharge does not trigger these time bars.

Related Guides

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Bankruptcy Dismissed - What Now?

File Bankruptcy Again Guide

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

The automatic stay is a court order that takes effect immediately when you file bankruptcy. It stops most collection actions, lawsuits, foreclosures, repossessions, wage garnishments, and creditor harassment. It remains in effect until the case is closed or the debt is discharged.

## What to Do If Your Bankruptcy Is Denied or Dismissed
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/what-to-do-if-denied.html

bankruptcydenied.com
☰

Home
Ch. 7 Denial
Means Test
Bad Faith
Prior Dismissal
Incomplete Filing
Fraud
What to Do
FAQ

What to Do If Bankruptcy Is Denied

Denial is not always the end. You may be able to refile, convert chapters, appeal, or pursue alternative debt relief.

Home›bankruptcydenied.com›What to Do If Your Bankruptcy Is Denied or Dismiss

Understand why it happened

The first step is understanding exactly why your case was denied or dismissed. The reason determines your options:

ReasonBest Option

Incomplete paperworkGather documents and refile

Means test failureConvert to Chapter 13 or wait and refile

Bad faith / abuseAddress underlying issues, wait 180 days if barred, then refile

Prior discharge time barWait for the bar to expire (use 1328f.com to check)

Discharge denied (fraud)Consult an attorney - very limited options in current case

Plan not confirmed (Ch. 13)Amend plan and resubmit, or convert to Chapter 7

Option 1: Refile

If your case was dismissed (not discharge denied), you can usually refile. Check for any refiling bars under § 109(g). Be aware that under § 362(c)(3)-(4), repeat filings within a year get reduced automatic stay protection.

Option 2: Convert chapters

If your Chapter 7 case is at risk of dismissal for means test failure, you can convert to Chapter 13 under 11 U.S.C. § 706(a). Conversely, if your Chapter 13 plan cannot be confirmed, you may be able to convert to Chapter 7 under § 1307(a) (if you qualify under the means test).

Option 3: Appeal

You can appeal a dismissal or discharge denial to the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel (BAP) or the district court within 14 days under Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 8002. Appeals are expensive and succeed only if the trial court made a clear legal error. Consult an experienced appellate attorney.

Option 4: Non-bankruptcy alternatives

If bankruptcy is not available or viable, consider:

Debt negotiation / settlement. Negotiate directly with creditors to reduce balances.

State court remedies. Some states offer debtor protections, homestead declarations, or wage garnishment limits.

Judgment-proof status. If you have no assets and no garnishable income, creditors cannot collect. Being judgment-proof is not a formal legal status, but it is a practical reality.

Debt management plans. Nonprofit credit counseling agencies can negotiate reduced interest rates and consolidated payments.

Most people who are denied can still find relief. Procedural dismissals are fixable. Means test failures lead to Chapter 13. Even after discharge denial, debts may become practically uncollectible. An experienced bankruptcy attorney can evaluate your specific situation and find the best path forward.

Related Guides

Can I File Bankruptcy Again?

Bankruptcy Dismissed - What Now?

File Bankruptcy Again Guide

Section 109(g) Filing Bar

A bankruptcy mill is a high-volume law firm that processes large numbers of bankruptcy cases with minimal attorney involvement. Cases are often handled by paralegals or software, leading to errors, missed deadlines, and poor outcomes for clients.

## Privacy Policy - bankruptcydenied.com
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/privacy.html

bankruptcydenied.com

Home
Privacy

Privacy Policy

How we handle your data. Short version: we don't sell it, share it, or use it for advertising.

Data We Collect

We use Google Analytics (GA4) to measure aggregate site traffic. This includes page views, session duration, approximate geographic region (country and city level), and device type. We do not collect names, email addresses, or personally identifiable information through analytics.

Aggregate event data from Google Analytics is also exported to Google BigQuery for research use. The BigQuery data is used only for internal trajectory analysis and network health reports, is not shared with third parties, and is not used for advertising.

What We Don't Do

We do not sell data. We do not run advertising. We do not collect financial information. We do not use retargeting. We do not share any user data with attorneys, law firms, creditors, debt collectors, or legal service providers.

Specifically, we do not enable Google Signals, Google Ads integration, User-ID collection, or any cross-device tracking feature in Google Analytics. GA4 operates in aggregate-traffic-measurement mode only on this site.

Cookies

We use only first-party cookies set by Google Analytics for aggregate traffic measurement. We do not use advertising cookies, tracking pixels, or third-party analytics cookies.

Third-Party Services

Google Analytics (GA4) - aggregate traffic measurement

Google BigQuery - aggregate event data warehouse for research use only; not shared, not used for advertising

Google Search Console - search query measurement (clicks, impressions, our own page rankings)

GitHub Pages - hosting

Contact Forms & Email

This site may link to contact forms or email addresses operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Any data you submit through those channels is handled under the Open Bankruptcy Project master privacy policy, which governs all sites in this network.

Children's Privacy

This site is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

Data Retention

Analytics data is retained for 14 months per Google's standard retention settings. After that window, individual event data is automatically deleted by Google; aggregate report metrics remain available.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any personal data we hold by contacting info@openbankruptcyproject.org. California residents have additional rights under CCPA. EU residents have additional rights under GDPR. All such requests are handled by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

Network Policy

This site is part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). The same privacy standards apply across every site in the network. The authoritative master policy is maintained at https://openbankruptcyproject.org/privacy.html.

Changes

We may update this policy from time to time. Changes are reflected on the master policy first and then mirrored across all network sites. Check the master policy for the most current version.

Effective: March 30, 2026  |  Updated: April 11, 2026

## About bankruptcydenied.com
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/about.html

bankruptcydenied.com

Home
About
Privacy

About bankruptcydenied.com

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

What This Site Is

bankruptcydenied.com is an educational resource operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). It's part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - a collection of free, public-interest sites that translate federal bankruptcy court data, statutes, and procedures into language ordinary people can use.

The Open Bankruptcy Project

The Open Bankruptcy Project builds free, open-source tools that make public bankruptcy court data accessible to the people it affects most - debtors, advocates, researchers, journalists, and policymakers. Every screening tool, analysis script, and dataset is published on GitHub. Anyone can audit, reproduce, or build upon the work without permission or payment.

Our research is derived primarily from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database covering all federal bankruptcy filings 2008 through 2024, cross-referenced with PACER docket data via the Free Law Project's RECAP archive and independent court-scraping tooling. Methodology and source code are public.

What This Site Is Not

This site is not a law firm. We do not represent clients, file bankruptcy cases, or give legal advice. We do not receive referral fees, affiliate commissions, or advertising revenue. We do not sell data.

If you need legal advice about your specific situation, consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney in your state.

Research Contributions

Our research supports two accepted suggestions to the Federal Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules:

Suggestion 26-BK-3 - procedural screening for 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f) re-filing eligibility

Suggestion 26-BK-5 - Rule 9037 / Form 121 / Form 309E1 amendments addressing systematic unredacted Social Security number exposure on federal bankruptcy dockets

Contact

General inquiries, data requests, research collaboration, and media: info@openbankruptcyproject.org

Privacy and Data Handling

See our privacy policy for details. Short version: aggregate analytics only; no data sold, no advertising, no attorney referrals, no financial information collected.

Home  ·  About  ·  Privacy  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project. Educational information only - not legal advice.

## Bankruptcy Denial in Alabama: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/states/alabama.html

← bankruptcydenied.com home

Bankruptcy Denial in Alabama: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Alabama residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Alabama?

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in Alabama can be denied in two different ways:

Case dismissed - the court throws out the entire case. No discharge. Debts survive.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Alabama federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Alabama-specific data matters.

Alabama Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Alabama. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,743 consumer bankruptcy cases from Alabama's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7478n/an/a

Chapter 131,265n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Alabama

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Alabama dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Alabama Means Test and Denial Risk

Alabama's single-person median income is $56,050, below the national average. Most filers here pass Part 1 of the means test on income alone. Denial for means-test failure is less common in Alabama than in high-income states.

Use the Alabama means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Dismissal rates in Alabama do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Alabama's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Alabama Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

## Bankruptcy Denial in Alaska: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/states/alaska.html

← bankruptcydenied.com home

Bankruptcy Denial in Alaska: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Alaska residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Alaska?

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in Alaska can be denied in two different ways:

Case dismissed - the court throws out the entire case. No discharge. Debts survive.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Alaska federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Alaska-specific data matters.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Alaska

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Alaska dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Alaska Means Test and Denial Risk

Alaska's single-person median income is $73,866, near the national midpoint. Filers close to the median should carefully compute their 6-month average - one high month can flip the result.

Use the Alaska means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Dismissal rates in Alaska do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Alaska's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Alaska Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

Related Alaska Resources

Alaska means test and income thresholds

Alaska bankruptcy exemptions

Bankruptcy Denial in Arkansas: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Arkansas residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Arkansas?

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Arkansas federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Arkansas-specific data matters.

Arkansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Arkansas. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 959 consumer bankruptcy cases from Arkansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 746296.7%3.3%

Chapter 1349760.9%39.1%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Arkansas

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Arkansas dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Arkansas Means Test and Denial Risk

Arkansas's single-person median income is $54,714, below the national average. Most filers here pass Part 1 of the means test on income alone. Denial for means-test failure is less common in Arkansas than in high-income states.

Use the Arkansas means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Arkansas's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 3.3% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Arkansas has a relatively low Chapter 13 dismissal rate (39.1%). Plans are more likely to reach completion here than in most states.

Dismissal rates in Arkansas do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Arkansas's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Arkansas Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

## Bankruptcy Denial in California: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/states/california.html

← bankruptcydenied.com home

Bankruptcy Denial in California: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for California residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in California?

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in California can be denied in two different ways:

Case dismissed - the court throws out the entire case. No discharge. Debts survive.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the California federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where California-specific data matters.

California Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for California. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 6,723 consumer bankruptcy cases from California's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 75,80898.4%1.6%

Chapter 1391538.8%61.2%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in California

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in California dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

California Means Test and Denial Risk

California's single-person median income is $79,253, well above the national average. More filers here will need to run the full Form 122A-2 (Part 2 expense deduction) rather than passing Part 1 on income alone. Above-median filers who fail the full means test face a presumption of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2), which the U.S. Trustee can raise even if the court does not.

Use the California means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

California's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 1.6% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

California Chapter 13 cases fail at a high rate (61.2% dismissal among resolved cases). Roughly half or more of filers who attempt a 3-5 year repayment plan never reach discharge. This is driven by the plan duration itself - job loss, medical events, or car trouble during the plan often end it. Filers considering Chapter 13 in California should take a hard look at whether Chapter 7 is available and preferable.

Dismissal rates in California do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether California's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your California Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

More filers here will need to run the full Form 122A-2 (Part 2 expense deduction) rather than passing Part 1 on income alone. Above-median filers who fail the full means test face a presumption of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2), which the U.S. Trustee can raise even if the court does not.

Use the District of Columbia means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Dismissal rates in District of Columbia do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether District of Columbia's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your District of Columbia Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

Bankruptcy Denial in Florida: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Florida residents.

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in Florida can be denied in two different ways:

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Florida federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Florida-specific data matters.

Florida Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Florida. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 724,38994.2%5.1%

Chapter 1321,61951.3%48.6%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Florida

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Florida dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Florida Means Test and Denial Risk

Florida's single-person median income is $69,876, near the national midpoint. Filers close to the median should carefully compute their 6-month average - one high month can flip the result.

Use the Florida means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Florida's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 5.1% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Florida Chapter 13 dismissal rate is 48.6%, in line with national averages. Completion is far from guaranteed - budget for realistic plan payments, not just the minimum that confirms the plan.

Dismissal rates in Florida do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Florida's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Florida Case Gets Denied

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

Bankruptcy Denial in Kansas: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Kansas?

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in Kansas can be denied in two different ways:

Case dismissed - the court throws out the entire case. No discharge. Debts survive.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Kansas federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Kansas-specific data matters.

Kansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Kansas. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 40,849 consumer bankruptcy cases from Kansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 718,67399.4%0.5%

Chapter 1322,17673.1%26.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Kansas

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Kansas dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Kansas Means Test and Denial Risk

Kansas's single-person median income is $69,197, near the national midpoint. Filers close to the median should carefully compute their 6-month average - one high month can flip the result.

Use the Kansas means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Kansas's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 0.5% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Kansas has a relatively low Chapter 13 dismissal rate (26.9%). Plans are more likely to reach completion here than in most states.

Dismissal rates in Kansas do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Kansas's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Kansas Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

## Bankruptcy Denial in Minnesota: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]
Source: https://bankruptcydenied.com/states/minnesota.html

← bankruptcydenied.com home

Bankruptcy Denial in Minnesota: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Minnesota residents.

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Minnesota?

Yes. Bankruptcy cases in Minnesota can be denied in two different ways:

Case dismissed - the court throws out the entire case. No discharge. Debts survive.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Minnesota federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Minnesota-specific data matters.

Minnesota Federal Bankruptcy Data

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Minnesota. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 395 consumer bankruptcy cases from Minnesota's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 737999.7%0.3%

Chapter 1316n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Minnesota

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Minnesota dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Minnesota Means Test and Denial Risk

Minnesota's single-person median income is $79,161, well above the national average. More filers here will need to run the full Form 122A-2 (Part 2 expense deduction) rather than passing Part 1 on income alone. Above-median filers who fail the full means test face a presumption of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2), which the U.S. Trustee can raise even if the court does not.

Use the Minnesota means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Minnesota's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 0.3% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Dismissal rates in Minnesota do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Minnesota's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Minnesota Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

Related Minnesota Resources

Minnesota means test and income thresholds

Minnesota bankruptcy exemptions

Full denial/dismissal FAQ

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Missouri Means Test and Denial Risk

Missouri's single-person median income is $64,972, near the national midpoint. Filers close to the median should carefully compute their 6-month average - one high month can flip the result.

Use the Missouri means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Missouri's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 0.8% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Missouri Chapter 13 dismissal rate is 44.7%, in line with national averages. Completion is far from guaranteed - budget for realistic plan payments, not just the minimum that confirms the plan.

Dismissal rates in Missouri do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Missouri's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

Bankruptcy Denial in Nevada: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

State-specific rules, federal bankruptcy filing data, and practical guidance for Nevada residents.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Nevada federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Nevada-specific data matters.

Dismissal rate is the single most important denial-risk metric for Nevada. A case that is dismissed - whether for incomplete paperwork, means test failure, or bad-faith findings - does not discharge your debts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 716493.4%5.9%

Chapter 137837.2%62.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Nevada

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Nevada dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Use the Nevada means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Nevada's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 5.9% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Nevada Chapter 13 cases fail at a high rate (62.8% dismissal among resolved cases). Roughly half or more of filers who attempt a 3-5 year repayment plan never reach discharge. This is driven by the plan duration itself - job loss, medical events, or car trouble during the plan often end it. Filers considering Chapter 13 in Nevada should take a hard look at whether Chapter 7 is available and preferable.

Dismissal rates in Nevada do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Nevada's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Nevada Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Most Common Denial Reasons in New Jersey

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in New Jersey dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

New Jersey Means Test and Denial Risk

New Jersey's single-person median income is $93,051, well above the national average. More filers here will need to run the full Form 122A-2 (Part 2 expense deduction) rather than passing Part 1 on income alone. Above-median filers who fail the full means test face a presumption of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2), which the U.S. Trustee can raise even if the court does not.

Use the New Jersey means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

New Jersey's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 2.7% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

New Jersey Chapter 13 cases fail at a high rate (68.8% dismissal among resolved cases). Roughly half or more of filers who attempt a 3-5 year repayment plan never reach discharge. This is driven by the plan duration itself - job loss, medical events, or car trouble during the plan often end it. Filers considering Chapter 13 in New Jersey should take a hard look at whether Chapter 7 is available and preferable.

Dismissal rates in New Jersey do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether New Jersey's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your New Jersey Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Oregon's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Oregon Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Use the Tennessee means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Tennessee's Chapter 7 dismissal rate of 4.5% is below the national average. Filers who complete their schedules correctly and attend the 341 meeting generally reach discharge here.

Tennessee Chapter 13 cases fail at a high rate (82.7% dismissal among resolved cases). Roughly half or more of filers who attempt a 3-5 year repayment plan never reach discharge. This is driven by the plan duration itself - job loss, medical events, or car trouble during the plan often end it. Filers considering Chapter 13 in Tennessee should take a hard look at whether Chapter 7 is available and preferable.

Dismissal rates in Tennessee do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Tennessee's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Tennessee Case Gets Denied

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

Discharge denied - the case stays open but specific debts (or all debts) are not wiped out under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 or Section 1328.

Both outcomes are decided by the Vermont federal bankruptcy court, which sits within the federal judiciary. The substantive rules are uniform nationally, but dismissal rates vary sharply by district - which is where Vermont-specific data matters.

Most Common Denial Reasons in Vermont

The denial reasons below are ranked by how often they appear in Vermont dismissal orders based on FJC data patterns and the national distribution of Section 707(b) and Section 727(a) rulings:

Incomplete paperwork - missing Schedules A-J, Statement of Financial Affairs, pay stubs, or tax returns. This is the single largest dismissal category nationwide.

Means test failure - presumption of abuse under Section 707(b)(2). More common in higher-income states.

Prior dismissal - Section 109(g) 180-day bar, or reduced automatic stay protection under Section 362(c).

Bad faith filing - Section 707(b)(3)(A) totality of the circumstances.

Fraud or concealment - Section 727(a) objections to discharge.

Vermont Means Test and Denial Risk

Vermont's single-person median income is $71,007, near the national midpoint. Filers close to the median should carefully compute their 6-month average - one high month can flip the result.

Use the Vermont means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Dismissal rates in Vermont do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Vermont's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.

If Your Vermont Case Gets Denied

Your options depend on why the case was denied:

Dismissed without prejudice (most common) - you can refile immediately, subject to automatic stay limitations under Section 362(c)(3). Fix whatever caused the dismissal first.

Dismissed with 180-day bar (Section 109(g)) - you must wait 180 days before refiling.

Discharge denied under Section 727 - you cannot get a Chapter 7 discharge of pre-petition debts through a later Chapter 7. Chapter 13 may still be available.

Converted to Chapter 13 - if dismissal was for means-test abuse under Section 707(b), you may be offered conversion rather than outright dismissal.

See our full denial response guide and the 109(g) refiling bar explainer.

Bankruptcy Denial in Virginia: Dismissal Rates and Denial Reasons [2026]

Can Bankruptcy Be Denied in Virginia?

Virginia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Virginia Means Test and Denial Risk

Virginia's single-person median income is $84,396, well above the national average. More filers here will need to run the full Form 122A-2 (Part 2 expense deduction) rather than passing Part 1 on income alone. Above-median filers who fail the full means test face a presumption of abuse under 11 U.S.C. Section 707(b)(2), which the U.S. Trustee can raise even if the court does not.

Use the Virginia means test calculator to check your Part 1 result before filing. If your income is above median, budget time for Part 2 expense calculations.

What Dismissal Rates Tell You

Virginia has a relatively low Chapter 13 dismissal rate (28.7%). Plans are more likely to reach completion here than in most states.

Dismissal rates in Virginia do not predict your individual case - they reflect the aggregate pattern across all filers. But they are a useful signal about how strict the district is on procedural compliance, how aggressively the U.S. Trustee's office operates, and whether Virginia's demographic mix pushes more filers into higher-risk categories.
